lesson.title: Subtracting Signals: The Difference Amplifier
lesson.summary: A single op-amp circuit that outputs a scaled copy of the voltage difference between two inputs, the building block that lets you measure a signal referenced to another signal instead of to ground.
lesson.body:
Many real signals are not naturally referenced to ground. A thermocouple, a strain gauge bridge, or a long audio cable produces a voltage that only makes sense as the difference between two wires, not as either wire measured alone against ground. If you tried to amplify just one of those wires with the inverting or non-inverting amplifier from earlier chapters, you would faithfully amplify whatever noise or offset happened to sit on that wire right along with the real signal. What you actually want is a circuit that looks at both wires and outputs a scaled version of their difference, ignoring whatever the two wires have in common.

The difference amplifier does exactly that by combining the inverting and non-inverting amplifier configurations onto a single op-amp. One input voltage, V1, drives the inverting input through a resistor R1, with a feedback resistor R2 completing that side exactly as in an ordinary inverting amplifier. The other input voltage, V2, drives the non-inverting input through a resistor R3, and a fourth resistor R4 ties that non-inverting input to ground, forming a voltage divider. Because the op-amp forces its two inputs to the same voltage through negative feedback, the same assumption used for every op-amp circuit so far, the non-inverting side sets a reference that the inverting side's feedback loop then has to match, and the resistor network performs the subtraction.

When the two resistor pairs are matched, R1 equal to R3 and R2 equal to R4, the algebra collapses to a clean result: Vout equals (R2 divided by R1) times (V2 minus V1). The ratio R2/R1 is simply the differential gain, the same gain expression as the plain inverting amplifier, only now it multiplies the difference between two inputs instead of a single input measured against ground. This matching condition is not a minor detail. If the ratios are even slightly unequal, some of whatever V1 and V2 have in common leaks into the output instead of canceling, which is precisely the imperfection that CMRR, covered later in this unit, measures.

Consider R1 = R3 = 1 kilohm and R2 = R4 = 10 kilohm, giving a differential gain of R2/R1 = 10. Suppose V1 = 2V and V2 = 3V. Then Vout = 10 times (3V minus 2V) = 10 times 1V = 10V. Now suppose instead both inputs carry the same 5V signal, V1 = V2 = 5V, a purely common-mode condition with no real difference between the wires. Ideally Vout = 10 times (5V minus 5V) = 10 times 0V = 0V. The amplifier produces no output at all, correctly recognizing that there is no genuine difference signal to amplify, even though each individual wire sits at a hefty 5V.

The difference amplifier's one real weakness is input impedance. Both V1 and V2 drive directly into resistor networks, so any source with meaningful internal resistance, like a sensor or a microphone, gets loaded down and partially loses its signal before it even reaches the op-amp. Fixing that loading problem, while keeping the difference-taking behavior developed here, is exactly what the instrumentation amplifier is built to do next.
